## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. A collapsible section opens with +++ followed by its title, and closes with +++ on its own line:

+++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

+++
</system-reminder>

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. ## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

Tools accept human-readable references, so you rarely need to look up IDs first: issue identifiers such as LIN-123, project identifiers such as P-ENG-12, team names or keys, user names or emails, and "me" for the authenticated user. Only call list_teams, list_users, or similar tools when a reference is ambiguous or unknown.

Use list_issues for structured queries, such as the issues assigned to "me" in a team, status, label, project, or cycle, and its query parameter for keyword search. Results are paginated: when hasNextPage is true, pass the returned cursor to fetch the next page rather than assuming the first page is complete.

Statuses and labels belong to teams and differ between them. When you are not sure which values a team supports, call list_issue_statuses or list_issue_labels for that team before filtering or setting them.

get_issue does not include the issue's discussion. Call list_comments with the issue ID to read comments, including inline comments on the description.

Issue descriptions, comments, and documents often embed screenshots and other uploads as markdown images. Pass that markdown to extract_images to view them. Read issue attachments with get_attachment; files uploaded in comments are returned in the attachments field of list_comments. Linear upload URLs are signed and expire after a few minutes, so fetch them again instead of reusing old URLs.

Tools named save_* both create and update: omit id to create a new entity, or pass id to update an existing one. When updating, pass only the fields you want to change. To edit part of a long issue description or document, pass patch instead of resending the full content.

Before creating an issue, check with list_issues whether a matching issue already exists, to avoid duplicates. When creating, team is required.

The labels parameter of save_issue replaces the issue's full label set. To add or remove individual labels without dropping others, use addLabels and removeLabels instead.

Markdown content supports user mentions with @displayName (for example @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the markdown it returns; do not inline base64 data.

Write issue descriptions for people to read. Keep sentences short, and use the same term for the same concept throughout.

Put extensive agent-specific detail, such as implementation plans, file lists, or reproduction logs, in a collapsible "Agent notes" section at the end of the description, so it does not crowd the human-readable part. +++ Agent notes

Details for agents go here.

    The fact store is flat per repository (branch became a record field).
    factstore.Load/Write lost their branch parameter, so the write-back and
    the provenance read follow. Two consequences stated rather than
    inherited: the write-back's presence check is now repository-wide,
    which is the right reading of a content-derived id since it never
    depended on a branch; and the provenance walk is repository-wide,
    because an ancestor recorded on another branch is still an ancestor and
    filtering the walk by branch would answer "nothing replaced this" when
    something did. provenance --branch is therefore gone, the per-branch
    "it is on another branch" hint is gone with the partitioning that made
    it necessary, and provenanceNode carries Branch so a reader can still
    see where each memory in a chain came from.

5. Any other remnants of: vector/embedding code, conversation vector state ("vector_state": "removed"), CAS client, hosted proposals queue, branch-partitioned store code paths, MCP framework remnants (the user says "mcp framework" was removed, but brain capabilities still list "mcp" as a feature — check what internal/cli has for MCP and whether it is alive).

input.description: Audit retrieval hot path
input.prompt:
Repo: /Users/evisdrenova/conductor/workspaces/entire-brain/juba (Go CLI; "entire brain" is a local memory/retrieval system for coding agents). The team wants brain to be faster and smarter. Current state: BM25 lexical is the only ranking (semantic retrieval removed); the live store here has ~24,700 facts across what used to be 170 branches (now a flat store with branch as a record field); `entire brain recall`, `entire brain brief`, and `entire brain status` are the hot commands; status/brief currently print warnings like "memory count does not match the manifest … run `entire brain refresh`" and "seed is stale; run entire brain refresh".

Search breadth: very thorough. Read the retrieval pipeline and report on performance and quality:
1. `internal/cli/internal/retrieval` (retrieve.go, guard.go), `internal/cli/internal/factstore`, `internal/cli/internal/manifest`, `internal/cli/internal/brainstore` (36 files), `internal/cli/internal/historystore`: for one `recall` query, what I/O happens? Does it scan every fact file on disk, load the whole store into memory, or use an index (SQLite? the capabilities report says sqlite_driver: sqlite)? Where is BM25 computed — precomputed index or per-query scoring over all docs?
2. `brain brief`: what sources does it assemble (history grep over session JSONL files? docs index? facts?), and which steps look expensive (e.g. scanning sessions/main/*.jsonl per call)?
3. Freshness/manifest: why would the manifest chronically drift from the store (declared 24728 vs readable 24735)? Is `refresh` manual-only, or is there a watcher/daemon that should keep it current (internal/cli/command/watch, parentwatch)? Is there a cheap incremental path, or does refresh rebuild everything?
4. recall's "ranking, proposal, receipt, blind-spot, evidence, and query-expansion arms" (mentioned in internal/cli/facts_commands.go factsCommandConfig): enumerate these arms, what each adds to a query, and which look expensive or of dubious value.
5. Any caching between invocations (the CLI is a short-lived process — does every call re-read/parse everything?). Any obvious O(n) per-query work that grows with fact count or session count.
6. Quality levers: how are facts deduplicated/superseded (factmerge), is there decay/aging, and is there anything that filters the 24k distilled facts for quality at recall time?

Report ~10 findings max, most valuable first, each with file:line anchors and a one-line "so what" (speed or quality impact). No search narration.

- `dash` is a terminal UI: `command/dash` (506) plus the full-screen part of `internal/tui`.
- `viz` is a browser UI: `command/viz` (1,373) plus the embedded `webui/dist` (about 104 KB of hand-written JS/CSS). CI runs Node and Playwright jobs for it (`test.yml:44,62-66`).
- `inspect graph-ui` writes a static HTML page from inline templates (`renderSemanticGraphHTML`, `semantic_graph.go:1046`).
- Potential: drop `graph-ui` (it overlaps `viz`). Then pick either `dash` or `viz`. Dropping `viz` also removes the module-root `webui.go` embed and the Node/Playwright jobs.

**5. Multi-repo workspaces, about 5.7k LOC.**
- Files: `workspace.go` (2,224), `internal/cli/workspace/` (8 files, 1,815), `workspace_patterns.go` (750), `pattern_workspace_cli.go` (114), `patterns/workspace_*` (828), plus the `setup --workspace` flag and the workspace path in `watch`.

- Files: `facts_eval.go` (1,266), `facts_eval_gen.go` (653), `facts_eval_compare.go` (504), `facts_eval_arms.go` (129), `history_eval.go` (422), `bench_scale.go` (820), `command/bench` (221).

content.text:
Survey complete — three explorers plus Brain recall, verified against current source. The short version: **the worst problems on this machine are a stale installed binary, not the code; the biggest code wins are hot paths that re-read the whole fact store several times per call; and about 40k LOC of removable surface remains, led by the pattern subsystem, the `inspect` group, and multi-repo workspaces.**

## 0. Do first: your local brain runs an old build

`~/.local/bin/entire-brain` was built Oct 26, before the proposal removal, the MCP removal, and the flat fact store (Nov 2). That one fact explains most of the noise:

- The phantom `proposals: 59329` and the `mcp` capability come from the old binary. Current source writes neither.
- The local store is still 176 per-branch `facts.ndjson` files: 24,735 lines but only **~2,834 unique facts**. Every `recall`/`brief` parses and merges all 24,735 lines. A rebuild plus one `refresh` migrates to the flat store and cuts every fact read ~9x.
- The "manifest behind the store" warning is 7 staged candidates the old binary does not count; fixed Oct 26 in source.

Two real operational gaps remain even with a new build: the watcher defers full refresh while the worktree is dirty, so in Conductor it effectively never runs; and the brain is keyed by origin remote and shared across all 8 worktrees, so the "seed is stale" warning can never clear for more than one of them. Both deserve fixes (refresh despite dirty tree from the committed side; ancestor-based seed freshness).

## 1. Faster: stop re-reading the store

- `recall` merges the full store up to **three times** per query (`facts_read_cmd.go:103`, `integrity.go:298`, and `blind_spot.go:51` on empty results) and spawns ~4 git subprocesses. BM25 is recomputed from scratch per query — facts never touch SQLite (the FTS index is history/docs only). Fine at 2.8k facts, but one shared merge plus a digest-keyed postings sidecar would make it O(small).
- `brief` is the slowest path: it runs the full non-lightweight status (graph subprocess, another full store merge, retrieval audit at `agent_surface.go:4508-4669`), then loads the store *again* for its facts section, and for some task wordings reads up to 2,500 repo files. Use the lightweight status and reuse the already-loaded facts.
- `refresh` does 3–4 full store loads plus a whole-file rewrite, and rebuilds the doc index every run even when nothing changed.
- The vitality receipt costs a `git rev-parse` plus a locked append on every recall, and by design never affects ranking. Either feed it into ranking or stop paying for it.

## 2. Smarter: quality bugs and missing priors

- **Live quality bug in brief's history section**: the raw scan reads derived indexes (`docs/index.json`, `entities/index.json` — the latter matches almost any identifier), and raw hits are merged *ahead of* the FTS-ranked history, pushing ranked results out (`agent_surface.go:1709`, `:5495`). There are also eval-tuned hacks in there (an "ultron" exclusion, a +100 boost for "LIMIT" queries). Skip derived dirs and merge indexed results first.
- `recall` has no recency prior and no decay — the 90-day half-life exists but only on `query`, never on `recall`. Confidence is 1.00 on 95% of facts, so it carries no signal. The flat +4 bonus for closed-negative facts applies to ~17% of the corpus regardless of relevance.
- Near-duplicate facts below the old confidence threshold stay active as cross-linked pairs; 1,910 active records carry `related_ids` and reach recall un-collapsed. Collapsing those pairs is probably the single best relevance lever.
- `--expand` spawns an LLM on every call because its cache path is `""` (`facts_commands.go:82`) — results are never saved.

## 3. Removal candidates, ranked

| Candidate | Size | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Compact brief v1/v2/v3 serializers — no flag or caller can reach them | ~1.4k LOC + 2.9k test | Delete outright |
| `semantic_relevance.go` — zero callers | 255 LOC | Delete |
| `factmerge` confidence threshold / `ApplyActions` — test-only; production reconcile ignores confidence; comments still cite the removed `facts review` | ~80 LOC + tests | Delete, with the `--confidence` flag |
| Proposal/branch leftovers: `Proposals` counters, a `"proposals"` help entry in `root.go:250`, always-zero branch-count prints, and legacy-dir cleanup that can never delete orphan `proposals.ndjson`/`vitality`/`embeddings` (retained forever) | ~small code, 5.8 MB disk | Delete fields; teach cleanup the orphan names |
| `inspect` group — 16 verbs over a local copy of the code graph Brain no longer owns; `search-graph` is literally the same function as `inspect code`; agentsetup already points agents at `entire graph` | ~13k LOC | Delegate `context`/`impact`/`tests` to Graph, drop the rest |
| Pattern subsystem — episodes/corpus feed brief, but themes, lessons, conventions, deep dossiers, skill synthesis, and cross-repo families are opt-in agent runs | ~5k of 16.4k LOC | Quarantine or drop the opt-in half |
| Three browse UIs: `dash` (TUI), `viz` (web UI + Node/Playwright CI jobs), `inspect graph-ui` (static HTML) | ~2–3k LOC + CI | Drop `graph-ui`; pick one of `dash`/`viz` |
| Multi-repo `workspace` — 13 subcommands mirroring the single-repo ones | ~5.7k LOC | Product call; removing it also takes the cross-repo pattern code |
| Hidden eval/bench harnesses compiled into the shipped binary (`memories eval*`, `history-eval*`, `bench`) | ~4k LOC | Move to `tools/` or a build tag |
| `memory abstract` — ships disabled; `purgeSessionAbstracts` is already dead | 2.6k LOC | Remove or commit to it |
| Migration/tombstone code (legacy layouts, `init-agents`/`publish` tombstones, deprecated no-op flags, `vsearch` alias) | ~1.5k LOC | Sweep after a version cutoff |
| `benchmarks/` (12 MB of historical experiment archives) and 4.9 MB of images in `docs/` | 17 MB | Move out of the repo |

Structurally, `internal/cli` is still a 183-file, 87k-LOC flat package; the extracted `command/*` shells hold only ~7% and call back into the monolith through `Deps` seams. The removals above would shrink four of its five largest files.

## Bounds from recorded decisions (so we don't relitigate)

- Embedder/vector reinstatement was explicitly rejected (trail #278, cgo stripped in #416; facts beat embedded chunks 12.6–14x on useful-tokens). "Smarter" should mean better lexical ranking and dedup, not embeddings.
- Topic-specific ranking bonuses were removed after a flat 23-task offline comparison — any ranking change (recency prior, pair-collapsing, dropping the +4 bonus) should go through the same eval harness before landing.
- `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` is a deliberate keep.
- One recorded bug I checked is already fixed: pulled teammate facts do reach the store now (`hosted_sync.go:506-542`).

If you want an order: rebuild + refresh today; then the brief history-merge bug and recall's triple-merge (small diffs, immediate effect); then the `inspect`-to-Graph delegation and the pattern quarantine as the two big LOC reductions. Happy to turn any slice of this into a Linear issue or start on the quick deletions.

content.text:
Both verified against current source. Here is the overview.

## Fix 1 — Brief's history section ranks junk above ranked history (quality bug)

**What happens now.** When `brief` assembles its "history" section it has two sources: the FTS5-ranked history index, and a raw text scan of the brain directory. At `internal/cli/agent_surface.go:1705-1709` the raw scan runs unconditionally (it gets `nil` as "existing matches", so it never knows the index already filled the limit), and `mergeBrainBriefHistoryMatches(limit, rawMatches, indexedMatches)` fills the result in group order — raw hits first, ranked hits only into whatever slots remain.

**Why it is bad.** The raw scan's skip list (`agent_surface.go:5023-5040`) excludes history, facts, patterns, and seed, but not `docs/` or `entities/`. So it matches inside derived index files — `docs/index.json` (1.5 MB) and `entities/index.json` (520 KB on a single line, which matches almost any identifier). Those junk excerpts then displace the FTS-ranked session history in every brief. There are also two eval-tuned hacks in the raw scorer (an "ultron" path exclusion and a +100 boost for queries containing "LIMIT", around `:5443-5476`) that should not survive a cleanup.

**The fix.** Three small changes: add `docs/` and `entities/` (derived artifacts generally) to the skip list; reverse the merge order so indexed results fill first and the raw scan only tops up; skip the raw scan entirely when the index already fills the limit. Deleting the two scorer hacks is a judgment call — per the recorded precedent (topic bonuses were removed after a flat A/B), ranking changes should go through the offline eval harness.

**Effort and risk.** Small diff, one file plus tests. The risk is that some brief outputs change, which is the point; the eval harness (`memories eval`) is the check.

## Fix 2 — Recall parses the fact store up to three times per query

**What happens now.** One `recall` does: a full `factstore.Load` (`internal/cli/command/facts/facts_read_cmd.go:103`), then `factstore.InspectBrain` (`:139`) which loads and merges the store *again* for the integrity check, and on an empty result `EmptyResultBlindSpot` (`:221`, `:243`) loads it a *third* time to explain the miss. On top of that: BM25 is rebuilt from scratch per query (`facts_bm25.go` re-tokenizes every fact twice and rebuilds document frequencies), and the receipt write adds a `git rev-parse HEAD` subprocess plus a locked append that nothing ever reads for ranking.

**Why it matters less than it did yesterday.** Before the migration this meant parsing 24,735 NDJSON lines two or three times. Now it is a 3.4 MB `store.json`, and recall measures ~0.27s — so this is no longer an emergency. It is still the right structural fix: the cost returns as the corpus grows, and every redundant load is also a redundant lock acquisition and failure path.

**The fix.** Load once and pass the loaded store to the integrity check and the blind-spot explainer — the data is identical, only the call sites differ. Optionally drop the per-recall receipt write (or batch it), since it is recorded as never affecting ranking. A persisted BM25 postings sidecar keyed by the store digest is the step after that, worth doing only if measurement says tokenization dominates at real corpus sizes.

**Effort and risk.** The single-load refactor is mechanical: `Load`, `InspectBrain`, and the blind-spot path live behind the `facts.Config`/`Deps` seams, so it is mostly threading a value through. Low risk; existing recall tests cover the behavior.

**Order.** Fix 1 first — it changes what agents actually see in every brief. Fix 2 is latency and predictability, and its first half is a near-trivial diff.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.0/skills/test-driven-development

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

**"Other tests" means the project's suite, not just your file.** A
green run of the test you wrote is not a green suite. Before you call
the change done, run the project's test command (bare `pytest`,
`npm test`, `cargo test` — whatever the repo uses) even when your task
named only one test file. A scope statement in your task bounds the
deliverable, not your verification. Any failure that run shows —
including one you didn't cause — goes in your report by name; a red
test you watched scroll past and didn't mention is a report falsified
by omission.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

When writing or changing any test, read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) for the rules that keep tests honest:
- Name the production change that would make the test fail — before writing it
- Assert on real behavior, never on mock behavior
- Keep test-only code in test utilities, out of production classes
- Understand a dependency's side effects before mocking it

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests written after pass immediately — which proves nothing. They may test the wrong thing, test the implementation instead of the behavior, or miss the edge case you forgot. You never watched it fail, so you never proved it can catch the bug. Test-first forces that failure. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" | Tests-after answer "what does this do?"; tests-first answer "what should this do?" Tests written after are biased by the code you already wrote — you verify the cases you remembered, not the ones you'd have discovered. Coverage without proof the tests work. |
| "Already manually tested" | Manual testing is ad-hoc: no record of what you covered, no way to re-run it when the code changes, easy to forget cases under pressure. "Worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive. Automated tests run the same way every time. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy — that time is already spent either way. The real choice: rewrite with TDD (high confidence) vs. keep it and bolt tests on after (low confidence, likely bugs). Keeping code you can't trust is the waste. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD IS the pragmatic path: catches bugs before commit, prevents regressions, lets you refactor without fear. "Pragmatic" shortcuts mean debugging in production — slower, not faster. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

		Test:       "TestRootCommandPatternsLifecycleAndPrivacyFailures",
		Diagnostic: "refresh did not publish corpus",
		Package:    "./internal/cli",
	},
	{
		Name:       "mirror must delete facts of a removed checkpoint",
		File:       "internal/cli/facts_mirror.go",
		Before:     "\t\t\tif stripped > 0 && len(remaining) == 0 {",
		After:      "\t\t\tif false && stripped > 0 && len(remaining) == 0 {",
		Test:       "TestRefreshMirrorsCheckpointDeletion",
		Diagnostic: "anchored to the deleted session survived",
		Package:    "./internal/cli",
	},
	{
		Name:       "brief must preserve raw-only matches",
		File:       "internal/cli/agent_surface.go",
		Before:     "rawMatches, rawErr := rawHistoryMatcher(status.Brain.Path, task, nil, briefOpts.limit, rawProfile)",
		After:      "_ = rawProfile\n\t\t\trawMatches, rawErr := []brainTextMatch(nil), error(nil)",
		Test:       "TestRawHistoryFallbackRetainsFallbackOnlyMatch",
		Diagnostic: "end-to-end brief lost fallback-only match",
		Package:    "./internal/cli",
	},
	{
		Name:       "mirror must sweep abstracts of a removed checkpoint",
		File:       "internal/cli/facts_mirror.go",
		Before:     "\t\tif !liveRefs[entry.Artifact.SessionRef] {",
		After:      "\t\tif false && !liveRefs[entry.Artifact.SessionRef] {",
		Test:       "TestMirrorSweepsAbstractsOfMissingSessions",
		Diagnostic: "want one abstract and one receipt removed",
		Package:    "./internal/cli",
	},
}

still fills; it fails if the ranker dedup is ever removed.

EOF
